1:
When the ordinance was given is answered two ways that cannot both stand. Gill puts it back before Sinai was left, following Aben Ezra, and reports the tradition that the heifer was slain by Eleazar the day after the tabernacle was erected, the law being merely repeated here. Keil makes it a response to the present emergency: the traditional purifications sufficed while mortality stayed within natural limits, but when death prevailed to a hitherto unheard-of extent in consequence of the sentence pronounced by God, defilements were so crowded together that the whole congregation risked infection with the uncleanness of death and the forfeit of its vocation as a holy nation — and this law furnished the remedy.

Why the victim was a red heifer draws three quite different answers. Clarke reaches for Egypt twice: a heifer, probably against the Egyptian superstition that held them sacred and worshipped Isis under this form — the likelier since males were generally preferred for sacrifice yet here the female is chosen — and red, because red bulls were sacrificed to appease the demon Typhon among the Egyptians. Henry looks to rarity, the colour making it the more remarkable, and cites the Jewish rule that if but two hairs were black or white it was unlawful; then turns it typologically, that Christ as man was the son of Adam, red earth, and is found red in his apparel, red with his own blood and with his enemies'. Wesley takes the colour as shadowing sin's bloody nature and the blood of Christ, and on the untouched neck offers two readings — that Christ was free of all obligation to the law until for our sakes he put himself under it, or that he was not forced to take our burden but chose it, bound with no cords but those of his own love.

Who actually killed the heifer is a flat contradiction. Calvin makes it the priest's peculiar office, the people offering vicariously by his hand, and draws the parallel that even now, though we set Christ before God's face to propitiate him, Christ himself must interpose as priest. Keil says the opposite in as many words: it was not the priest's duty to slay the sacrificial animal but the offerer's, here the congregation's, which would appoint one of its own number, and all the priest had to do was sprinkle the blood. On why Eleazar rather than Aaron they agree — the work defiled, and the high priest was to be kept from all uncleanness of death — though Gill adds a second motive, to inure Eleazar to his office.

That the whole rite fell outside the camp is explained doctrinally by two and structurally by one. Calvin takes the removal as the sign of a curse, the heifer being an atonement, and points to Christ suffering outside the gate; then he guards the inference: lest the heifer be thought polluted by the curse, God showed her blood sacred by commanding it sprinkled seven times toward the altar, which nothing unclean might profane — and completes the figure, that Christ was made a curse for us without loss of purity. Keil explains the arrangement by its purpose: in every congregational sin-offering the animal was burnt outside the camp, but here the whole act was, because the design was not to receive the congregation into fellowship with the God present at the altar but to provide an antidote to the infection of death. Ellicott places the sprinkling opposite the tabernacle entrance but outside the camp; Wesley reads the preposition as merely toward it, Eleazar standing at a distance and turning to look, since being defiled he could not approach. Calvin states the aim of the whole: to make the people reflect on their impurity, and to teach them that men inquire in vain in themselves for remedies, since purity can only proceed from the sanctuary.
5:
The paradox — that the ashes purify while everyone who handles them is defiled — Calvin states as an apparent discrepancy and resolves twice over. The heifer was sacred to God and pure, yet the priest was polluted by touching it; these accord well, he says, because the defilement ought to have struck the people forcibly and taught them the more to abominate sin, and because the requirement that only a clean man gather the ashes, and only into a clean place, showed that the impurity was extraneous and adventitious — the sacrifice being accounted unclean precisely because it was destined to purge away uncleanness. Keil reaches the same place by rejecting a rival account: the officiants became unclean not through having acted for unclean persons and so shared their uncleanness, but through the uncleanness of sin and death which had passed to the sin-offering, as the man who led away the goat was defiled by the sins laid on it. Gill names the same parallel and adds an application no one else risks, that the defilement may point at the sin of the priests and people in putting Christ to death, from which there was nevertheless cleansing. Wesley divides the lesson in two: it teaches the imperfection of the Levitical priesthood, in which the priest was defiled by his own work, and shows Christ, having no sin of his own, reputed by men and judged by God a sinful person by reason of ours.

On the cedar, hyssop and scarlet the readings are emblematic and functional. Ellicott assigns each a meaning — cedar the emblem of fragrance and incorruption, hyssop of purification, scarlet both of sin, to which the prophet compares it, and of the blood which is the life — and notes that all three were used in cleansing the leper, as Gill and Wesley also observe. Calvin is interested in why they were burnt with the victim rather than in what they stand for: so that the sprinkling of the blood might be conjoined with that of the water, since without this visible sign the Israelites would not have known clearly that they were washed not by water only but by the offering of the sacrifice. He draws a second inference from the materials themselves, that since cedar's scent is precious and hyssop has a cleansing property, the victim is shown pure although it bore their sins with the curse.

Gill alone supplies the ritual as the Jews preserved it. The wood — cedar, ash, fir and fig — was laid in the form of a tower with holes opened in it. When the three materials were brought the priest asked three times of each, is this cedar wood, is this hyssop, is this scarlet, and was answered yes three times to each. Against defilement he was separated from his own house seven days beforehand and sprinkled daily with the blood of every sin offering, and a causeway on double arches ran from the temple to the Mount of Olives over the Kidron lest an unseen grave lie in the way. The ashes were pounded and sifted in stone sieves.

Calvin defends his own rendering of the phrase for purification, holding the water named from separation as well as from expiation. Wesley explains the term from the condition of those it served, appointed for cleansing them who for uncleanness are separated from the congregation, and glosses the Hebrew as an offering for sin, or rather a means of expiation, which typified the purification our Lord made by his death. Clarke states the mechanics plainly: the ashes were kept to be mixed with water and sprinkled on those who had contracted any legal defilement. Ellicott takes the stranger evangelically, the promise of remission through Christ reaching not the Jews and their children only but all that were afar off; Wesley identifies him soberly as a proselyte.
11:
That a dead man defiles for seven days where a dead beast defiles only until evening is felt by all, and answered four ways. Clarke turns it into an exclamation: how low does this lay man, seven times worse than the vilest animal, certainly designed to mark his peculiar impurity. Ellicott gives the reason compactly: the death of man was the wages of sin, so contact with his body carried a longer defilement. Calvin makes death a mirror of God's curse, since the corruption by which the image of God is defaced presents itself in every dead man — for unless we were altogether corrupt we should not be born to perish — and notes that no distinction is drawn between a man slain and a man who died in his bed. Henry alone declines to be satisfied, calling this one of the greatest burdens of the ceremonial law and one of the most unaccountable, precisely because touching the carcase of an unclean beast, or a living man under the greatest uncleanness, defiled only till evening and needed only common water. Gill fixes the boundaries from Aben Ezra: a man is meant and not a beast, and any man, Jew or Gentile.

Calvin extends the law beyond corpses. God taught his people by it that uncleanness is contracted by communication with the unfruitful works of darkness, which the Apostle calls dead works, either from their consequences or because, as faith is the life of the soul, unbelief keeps it in death; so the corpse, the bones and the grave designate whatever we bring from the womb until we are born again.

Clarke does the philology and then confesses defeat. The Hebrew for purifying oneself is literally to sin oneself, which he defends by an English parallel — to fleece, to bark and to skin mean not to add a fleece or a bark or a skin but to take one away, so to sin oneself is not to add sin but to remove it. On why a heifer, and a red one, when the Hebrews generally sacrificed males of any colour, he quotes Calmet's report that the rabbins, with all their boldness, who stick at nothing when they must explain what they do not understand, declare the cause entirely unknown, and that Solomon with all his wisdom could not find it out. Ellicott proposes a different construction of the days: the verse should read on the third day and on the seventh day so shall he be clean, and if he purify not himself on the third and on the seventh then he shall not be clean — which he supports from the Greek and Latin versions. Wesley finds significance in the earlier day, taking the third to typify Christ's resurrection.

On the penalty the two who face it hardest reach opposite emphases. Calvin argues that the severity of the punishment shows how pleasing purity is to God, then draws a line the text does not draw for him: a man who forgot the sprinkling on the third or seventh day might redeem his negligence by prolonging the term, since he only postponed his purification, whereas to enter the sanctuary in uncleanness was the capital crime, holy and profane being mixed and the altar polluted. He adds that what must be considered is the law's object, to teach the Israelites like children that no one polluting sacred things would be tolerated. Wesley qualifies the sentence more mildly, restricting it to transgression done presumptuously, since one who did it ignorantly had only to offer sacrifice; and he reads the closing clause as continuance in guilt, no longer to be washed away by this water but punished by cutting off. Keil states the mechanism without casuistry: the man who neglected the cleansing did not become clean, thereby defiled the dwelling of Jehovah, and was to be cut off from Israel.
14:
The scope of the law about the tent is settled at once by Gill: a tent is named only because the Israelites were then living in tents, as Aben Ezra remarks, and the law holds equally of a house. On the open vessel he narrows where Keil does not, reporting from the Targum of Jonathan, Jarchi and Maimonides that only an earthen vessel is meant. Keil leaves the class of vessel alone and explains the covering physically instead: what is intended is a vessel that has no lid fastened down with a string, the fastening being what prevents the smell of the corpse from penetrating it.

Gill also fixes the range of the defiling contacts. One slain with a sword in the open field means anyone who dies a violent death, whether by the sword or otherwise; and the Targum of Jonathan extends the uncleanness to whoever touched the sword itself. The phrase that follows, a dead body, he takes of one who dies a natural death, or suddenly, or in any other way — so that between the two clauses no manner of dying is left out.

On the ingredients of the sprinkling water the notes are lexical and doctrinal by turns. Ellicott corrects the rendering, that it should be the ashes of the burnt sin-offering, literally of the burning of the sin-offering. Keil describes the process — fresh water put upon the ashes in a vessel, and a bunch of hyssop dipped in it by a clean man on the third and seventh days — and attributes the choice of hyssop to its inherent purifying power, which is a physical claim rather than an emblematic one. Wesley presses the water alone and gets the most out of it: running water means water flowing from a spring or river, which is the purest, and manifestly signifies God's Spirit, to which water is often compared and by which alone true purification is obtained. He then turns the figure into a warning that no one else in the chapter makes — those who promise themselves benefit by the righteousness of Christ while not submitting to the influence of his Spirit deceive themselves, since they cannot be purified by the ashes otherwise than in the running water.

Who was to do the sprinkling Gill raises and answers against his own sources. The Targum of Jonathan makes the hyssop three stalks bound together and the man a clean priest; Gill accepts the first and rejects the second, holding that it does not seem necessary he should be a priest, but that anyone free from ceremonial pollution might do it. Keil, describing the same act, says only that a clean man was to take the hyssop, and so leaves the requirement where Gill leaves it.
19:
That the same water cleanses one man and defiles another is the difficulty the chapter ends on, and Wesley alone tries to say why. It is strange, he grants, but God would have it so for three reasons: to teach that the water did not cleanse by any virtue in itself or in the work done but only by virtue of God's appointment; to remind them of the imperfection of their priesthood and their ritual purifications, and so of the necessity of a better priest and sacrifice and way of purifying; and to show that the efficacy of God's ordinances does not depend on the person or quality of his ministers, since the very man who was polluted himself could and did cleanse others. He adds a note on the timing that keeps the paradox from being absolute: he that touched the water was unclean whether by sprinkling it or by being sprinkled with it, for even the man cleansed by it was not fully clean when sprinkled but only at the evening of that day.

Ellicott repairs the pronouns of the nineteenth verse, which the received rendering confuses. It should run that he — the clean person — shall purify him, the unclean person, and that he, the unclean person, shall then wash; so the two subjects of the sentence are kept apart. Gill has already noted that the Targum of Jonathan makes the sprinkler a clean priest, and reads the act simply as the water of purification applied to a man unclean in any of the ways the chapter has listed.

The last verse turns on a point of Hebrew that Calvin sets out fully. Others translate it, he reports, as whosoever toucheth an unclean thing shall be unclean; and since Hebrew has no neuter, both the relative and the noun may be taken either as masculine or as neuter, and neither sense would be unsuitable. He decides from the second clause that what is meant is the contagion by which unclean persons infect men, garments and other articles, and observes that those who had touched a body or bones or a grave were unclean not until evening only but for seven whole days. Gill and Wesley both settle the referent the same way without raising the grammatical question: the unclean person here is not the man defiled merely by handling the water, but the man under the greater uncleanness that the chapter has been legislating for throughout. Gill adds that it covers persons and things alike, any man or woman as well as any vessel, and reads it as denoting the spreading and infectious nature of sin, and how far sin and sinners are to be avoided. Keil records only the words of the verse.

Why the chapter should close on this note at all is answered by Calvin: it was added in conclusion lest the Jews murmur at the severity of the punishment, as though God would inflict death for a trifling sin — the closing verse showing instead how far the contagion reaches. Gill puts a limit on the word perpetual that the others leave alone, taking the statute as binding on Israel throughout their generations until the coming of the Messiah, when the ceremonial law that stood in divers washings and purifications was abolished. Wesley, consistent with his reading of the penalty earlier, glosses the man who does not purify himself as one who contemptuously refuses to submit to this way of purification.
